notes: SMALLEST HONEST CHANGE. Exists: four working recorders, a finished journal that renders beliefs, public statements and commitments, and — since the boundary was relaxed — a catalogue of real propositions in an ordinary save. Missing link: no caller in ordinary play; the only one is the demo. Smallest honest change: one caller, on one occasion, recording one private belief. What a player would then see: their own journal saying what they have come to think, and when — the first time anything in this game says a person was changed by something that happened to them.

This is lamontae's headline stated as a repository fact, and it is smaller than his summary suggests. He described the apparatus as built at both ends and connected at neither, which is exactly right, and one of the three obstacles has already gone: the catalogue can now carry the propositions a belief would point at.

Deliberately NOT asked here: what a belief should then DO — whether it moves a vote, a campaign or a relationship. That is downstream of an enacted law's effects machinery and belongs to the 'What passing a law actually does' lane. This record asks only what creates the record, not what reads it.
One of seven records from this sweep, and the one to answer first if only one is answered.
question: What act in an ordinary life should record that a person now holds a view, has said something publicly, or has changed their mind — and what supplies the occasion: a news story they read, a disaster in their state, a conversation, a vote they cast, or holding office through an event?

sourcesChecked.source: The four recorders in src/simulation/politics.ts, at origin/main 1c4992e8
sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: recordPublicPosition, recordPrinciple, recordPropositionExposure and recordSubjectKnowledge each have exactly ONE caller outside their own tests, and it is src/simulation/demo.ts. Nothing a player reaches records what anyone believes, says publicly, or knows. The writers exist and work; nothing calls them in a life.

The consumer is complete. It walks privateBeliefHistory and renders a sentence per proposition, walks publicPositionHistory and renders 'In public you said: ...', and walks campaignCommitments alongside them, all ordered and dated. It is ready for records that never arrive. It does not say what should create one.

Worth correcting an earlier reading of this record's author, because it removes an obstacle rather than adding one. The boundary no longer forbids propositions outright: it now counts only UNDECLARED ones, meaning those not carried by a registered pack. Since the us-state-and-local pack ships propositions, a production save can hold them, so the journal's proposition lookup would succeed. The catalogue is no longer the blocker. The only missing link is a writer in ordinary play.

title: What makes a person in the game form a view, and when
usableAnswer: One occasion to start with, and the rule for it: which act records a view, about which proposition, at what strength, and whether it is private belief, public statement or both. One is enough — the wiring is the hard part and the second occasion is cheap once the first exists. If the honest answer is that a person should form views only from things the game can already produce, say which of those things, because that bounds the first version.
whyItMatters: lamontae's own summary of his ten-year playtest is that the world diverges richly and nobody in it is changed by what happens. This is that sentence as a wiring gap. Both ends are built and neither is connected: nothing in ordinary play records a belief, and the surface that would show one is finished and waiting. It is the difference between a simulation of events and a game about people, and he rates relationships, personality and private goals his first priority.
